This catalogue uses \(D_{2n}\) for a group of order \(2n\); another common convention calls the same group \(D_n\). The abstract definition admits \(n=1,2\): it gives \(C_2\) and the Klein four-group, respectively. For \(n\geq3\), it is the symmetry group of a regular \(n\)-gon.

The group order is \(q-1\). For an invertible matrix, choose ordered linearly independent columns: after \(j\) choices, precisely \(q^j\) vectors are forbidden for the next column.

In size one the group is \(\mathbb F_q^\times\), cyclic of order \(q-1\), and hence simple exactly when \(q-1\) is prime. For size at least two and \(q>2\), the determinant has a proper nontrivial kernel, so simplicity fails. At \(q=2\), general and special linear groups coincide: size two gives \(S_3\), while every size at least three is simple.
The parameter \(q\) must be a prime power. This is a finite abstract group; the field and its vector space supply a construction, rather than a vector-space structure on the matrix group itself.

There are \((2^2-1)(2^2-2)=6\) invertible matrices. Every nonzero determinant equals one, so \(\mathrm{GL}_2(2)=\mathrm{SL}_2(2)\). Acting on the three nonzero vectors gives an injective map to \(S_3\): a matrix fixing all three vectors fixes a basis. Both groups have order six, so this is an isomorphism. The normal subgroup corresponding to \(A_3\) shows that it is not simple.

The independent-column count gives \((3^2-1)(3^2-3)=48\) elements. The determinant maps onto \(\mathbb F_3^\times\cong C_2\), with kernel \(\mathrm{SL}_2(3)\) of order 24. This proper nontrivial normal subgroup proves nonsimplicity.

The group order is \(1\). The determinant map from the general linear group onto \(\mathbb F_q^\times\) has this group as kernel. Dividing the general linear group order by \(q-1\) gives the formula.

In size one the group is trivial. For size \(m\geq2\), the center is \(\{\lambda I:\lambda^m=1\}\), of order \(\gcd(m,q-1)\). Its quotient is \(\mathrm{PSL}_m(q)\), which is simple except at \((m,q)=(2,2),(2,3)\). Thus the special linear group itself is simple exactly when its center is trivial and these two exceptions are absent.
